title: Make first contact
summary: Ask the practice CubeSat for a sensor reading and record it with its units.

steps: Press **Ask for a reading**.
Watch the mission log. Your question goes up to the satellite, and its answer comes back down.
Write down the three numbers you get. Copy the little letters after each number too, like °C or V.
beginner.check: You have three numbers, and each one has its unit next to it.
beginner.discuss: If a friend wrote "temperature 20" with no unit, what might you guess wrong?

steps: Press **Get sensor reading** and note the time the command was sent.
Record temperature (°C), bus voltage (V) and light (lx), plus the reply time in milliseconds from the log.
Take two more readings. Is the reply time always the same?
intermediate.check: Your table has three readings, each with units and a reply time in ms.
intermediate.discuss: What could make one reply slower than another on a real radio link?

steps: Send a sensors request. The log shows the command published on the `classroom/commands` broadcast and the reply group on `exchange.v1`.
Open **Raw telemetry** and record the `sequence`, `captured_unix_ms` and `source` fields along with the three values.
Take three readings and compute the mean round-trip time and its spread.
professional.check: You logged three JSON samples with sequence numbers and a mean RTT with its range.
professional.discuss: The reply carries a capture timestamp from the payload clock. What has to be true about the two clocks before you trust an age calculation?

title: Bring back a picture
summary: Start the test camera and count how many frames reach the ground.

steps: Press **Take pictures**.
Count the pictures as they arrive. Watch the white square move across the colours.
When it stops, write down how many pictures arrived out of 8.
beginner.check: You wrote down a number out of 8 and where the white square stopped.
beginner.discuss: Why is it useful that the camera sends lots of small pictures instead of one big one?

steps: Press **Start video** and time the burst from the first frame to the last.
Record the frame count, the burst duration and the time between frames.
Sketch the position of the marker in the first and last frames.
intermediate.check: You recorded 8 frames, the total time and the interval between frames.
intermediate.discuss: If each frame were 20 KB, how many kilobytes per second does this burst need?

steps: Start a video request. The reply is one MoQ group on `exchange.v1` with a JSON header frame, then 8 JPEG frames at 500 ms.
Note the estimated size of each frame and the total bytes listed in the log when the group completes.
Estimate the average bit rate of the burst in kbit/s.
professional.check: You have per-frame sizes, the group total and a bit-rate estimate with your working.
professional.discuss: Each frame is independently decodable. Compare that with H.264 inter-frame video over a lossy link.

title: Lose the signal on purpose
summary: Pause contact in the middle of a video burst and see what the ground keeps.

steps: Press **Take pictures**.
When a few pictures have arrived, press **Pause contact**. This is like the satellite flying out of sight.
Look at the mission log. How many pictures made it?
Press **Restore contact**, then ask for a new reading.
beginner.check: You know how many pictures arrived before contact stopped, and what came back afterwards.
beginner.discuss: A real satellite is only overhead for a few minutes. What would you do first when it comes back into view?

steps: Start a video burst and pause contact after two or three frames.
Record how many frames arrived and how the station marks the burst.
Restore contact and send a sensors request. Record how long it takes to recover.
intermediate.check: Your log shows a partial burst marked incomplete and a successful request after recovery.
intermediate.discuss: Should the ground station throw away an incomplete burst or keep it? Give one reason each way.

steps: Start a burst and pause contact mid-group. Note the last frame index received before the group stalls.
Restore contact and issue a new request. Confirm the reply line shows a new request id.
Explain why the station deduplicates request IDs and expires commands after 5 seconds.
professional.check: You identified the stall point, the recovery request ID and the purpose of the 5 s expiry.
professional.discuss: The real station rejects commands older than 5 s. What could go wrong if a delayed command ran after contact returned?

title: Fresh or historical?
summary: Find out when a reading stops counting as current, and why the station cares.

steps: Press **Ask for a reading** and look at the line under the numbers.
Wait and watch. When does **Fresh** change to **Historical**?
Pause contact. What does the line say now?
beginner.check: You found how many seconds a reading stays fresh.
beginner.discuss: Why is old information sometimes worse than no information?

steps: Get a reading and record the age at which the label changes to **Historical**.
Repeat with contact paused and compare.
Write one rule the next crew can use to decide whether a reading is current.
intermediate.check: Your rule names the 5 second limit and what happens while contact is paused.
intermediate.discuss: Would a 5 second limit work for a weather balloon logging once a minute? What would you choose?

steps: Get a reading and compare `captured_unix_ms` in **Raw telemetry** with the moment the label changes.
Confirm the threshold matches `MAX_AGE` in the station source (5000 ms).
Read `Sample::age_ms` in `src/main.rs` and describe what the station does with a sample whose capture time is ahead of the receiver clock.
professional.check: You confirmed the threshold and explained the future-timestamp rejection.
professional.discuss: How would you add clock uncertainty to the sample format so the ground can reason about it?

title: Light and shadow
summary: Take readings over a minute and explain why the light level sometimes drops to zero.

steps: Make a table with two columns, time and light.
Ask for a reading every 10 seconds for one minute.
Circle the rows where light is 0 lx.
beginner.check: Your table has at least six rows, and you circled the zeros.
beginner.discuss: Where could a satellite go that would make its light sensor read zero?

steps: Record time, light (lx) and temperature (°C) every 5 seconds for one minute.
Find how long the light stays on and how long it stays off.
Plot light against time on paper or in a spreadsheet.
intermediate.check: You measured the on and off durations and drew the pattern.
intermediate.discuss: The simulated cycle is 30 s. A real low-orbit pass around Earth takes about 90 minutes. What changes?

steps: Sample once per second for 40 s and record `sequence`, light and temperature.

Derive the light rule from the sequence numbers and confirm it against `Sample::synthetic` in the station source. In this demo the sequence is the time in seconds, like the station's `simulate` command; the installed classroom station counts requests instead.
Describe how you would replace the synthetic eclipse with one computed from an orbit model.
professional.check: You stated the rule (lit when sequence mod 30 is below 20) and verified it against the data.
professional.discuss: What inputs would an eclipse model need, and where would you get them for a real satellite?
